title: Six countries give environment ministries under 1% of budgets

needs.need: How the 2025 shares (Ecuador 0.08%, Argentina 0.04%) compare with the same countries' longer-run environment budget shares.
needs.accepts: A multi-year environment-budget share (average, peak or earlier year) as a percentage of the national budget for at least one of the six countries, with its period and a named source, so the 2025 figure can be read as a drop or as the norm. The 2025 figures alone do not meet it.

example.value: Argentina's environment budget averaged 0.13% of the national budget over the last decade and never exceeded 0.24%; Bolivia's averaged 0.56% over 16 years and never exceeded 1%.

needs.need: The history of funding cuts and institutional changes that left environmental agencies with weakened capacity.
needs.inStory: The spending declines span many years and governments, showing that environmental agencies have had low priority across political changes.
needs.accepts: A named source's country-specific account of prolonged funding cuts and a dated institutional or staffing change (a merger, dismissals, a downgraded ministry) and its effect on environmental protection.

example.value: In Ecuador, 16 years of declining funding, staff dismissals and institutional changes weakened biodiversity protection; the environment ministry was merged with the Energy Ministry in 2025.

needs.need: Where budget shortages are constraining protected-area staffing and conservation work.
needs.inStory: Mexico has only 717 people doing surveillance, monitoring, and conservation work in its protected areas, while Bolivia's 23 national protected areas face funding shortages.
needs.accepts: A country-specific example naming protected areas or conservation duties hit by shortages of funding or staff, credited to a named source. A regional biodiversity statistic alone does not meet it.

example.value: Ecuador's protected areas lack resources and personnel, weakening the state's ability to protect biodiversity.

needs.need: What governments or conservation bodies are doing to make up for the funding and staffing shortages, or which remedies have worked elsewhere.
needs.accepts: A named source's account of a concrete action under way or a remedy already tried to fund or staff environmental protection in one of the six countries or the region, naming the actor and the action and any reported result: for example a budget increase, a conservation trust fund or a debt-for-nature swap. A general call for more funding does not meet it.

example.value: Ecuador's 2023 debt-for-nature swap refinanced about $1.6 billion of debt and committed the savings to Galápagos marine conservation.

needs.need: What the reported environment budget shares count: ministry allocations or environmental spending across government, allocated or spent.
needs.accepts: An explanation credited to the analysis or another named source of what spending enters the environment-budget figure and the national-budget denominator, and whether the figures are allocations or actual expenditure.

notNeeded.why: This is a retrospective spending analysis with no single trigger; the causes belong in the account of long-term institutional erosion.
Neither the story nor its sources name a scheduled budget decision or deadline.

notes: Ecuador's ministry merger is evidence of institutional change, not a remedy for underfunding. A debt-for-nature swap or trust fund counts as a response only as money for conservation outside the ministry budget; it does not show that agency budgets rose.
